tagline.text: Seven beaches, cliff jumping and sunsets on a private Nasugbu coast

location.label: Location
location.text: Tali Beach Subdivision, Balaytigui, Nasugbu, Batangas

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,200–3,000 (per person for a day tour, excluding house stay)

children.text: Tali Beach is a private residential community in Balaytigui, Nasugbu, Batangas, where seven beaches lie along one stretch of coast. You can enter only through accommodation or a tour offered by residents or registered members, so it stays uncrowded, and it is a Manila-area beach known for cliff jumping and sunsets.
Tali Beach lies on the coast of Barangay Balaytigui in Nasugbu, Batangas, about
95km

southwest of Manila. People often speak of it as a single beach, but the name actually refers to the whole Tali Beach Subdivision, a private residential community with seven beaches inside: Main Beach, Sunset Beach, Secret Beach, Barrier Beach, Palm Beach, Coral Garden Beach and Marina Beach.

Its defining trait is that not just anyone can walk in. There is a guarded gate at the entrance, and visitors generally get in only by booking a beach house offered by a resident or registered member, or by joining a day tour connected to one. Showing up on your own is generally not allowed. In return, the beaches are far quieter and cleaner than public ones, and one reviewer reported almost no crowds even on a Sunday.

The highlights are cliff jumping and the sunset. From the rocky cliff near Sunset Beach you can pick a height and jump into the sea, and because the water opens to the west, the sky around dusk is beautiful. The surrounding Nasugbu area also holds Fortune Island, Punta Fuego, Hamilo Coast and Calayo, making Tali one pillar of a western Batangas coast trip from Manila.

Because it is a private community, visiting conditions and prices change often. Before you go, check the latest information with the accommodation or tour operator you booked, or with the Tali Beach Homeowners Group.
The best-known beach in the community, with fine white sand. Most of the beach houses cluster around it, so it works as a base for family and friend groups, and it is pleasant to walk barefoot.
You can go cliff diving near Sunset Beach. According to reviews there are three levels, about 6 ft (
2m
3m
) and 30 ft (
9m
), and if you are nervous it is best to start from the lowest one. It is also considered the best spot to watch the sunset.
Described as the longest of the seven beaches, it sits at the northwestern end of the community, next to Sunset Beach. There is plenty of room for photos or quiet relaxing.
Day tours usually start the morning at Palm Beach with swimming and photos, then move to Marina Beach to spend time at a relaxed pace. Marina Beach has an open view toward the sea.
You can rent kayaks and paddleboards. In a 2018 review a kayak cost about
per hour, so ask the operator for the current rate. Many guides advise asking locally about equipment rental.

The water in front of the beaches is decent for snorkeling, and diving is said to be possible in deeper water. Depending on the tour, life vests and goggles are lent out. Keep an eye on currents and waves on the day.

Renting a whole beachfront house with several rooms is the usual way to stay. Many houses let you walk barefoot onto the sand, and some have a swimming pool. The more people you bring, the lower the cost per person.

The sand color, waves and rocks differ a little from beach to beach, so it is fun to visit several in one day. The beaches are linked by community roads, so you move around by tour vehicle or as your house host directs.

items.title: Day tour route
items.subtitle: Early start, a round of the seven beaches

children.text: Leave Metro Manila. Many day tours gather near a shopping mall and travel by van.
Pass the Kaybiang (Kaibiang) Tunnel and stop for photos. You go through this tunnel if you come by the Cavite route.
Enter the community, change clothes, and swim and take photos at Palm Beach.
Move to Marina Beach and enjoy the sea.
Lunch time. Bring a packed lunch or eat a meal arranged by the tour operator.
Relax at Secret Beach, then head toward Sunset Beach for cliff jumping.
Move to Main Beach for a last swim and to clean up.
Watch the sunset from the beach, then leave for Manila.
This schedule is an example based on a 2018 day-tour review, and the order and times vary with the operator and the weather. Follow the itinerary of the operator you booked.

items.title: 2 days, 1 night beach house route
items.subtitle: Slow days at a beach house

children.text: Leave Manila early and reach the community entrance before lunch. Confirm your house host's instructions and the vehicle pass.
Check in at the house's check-in time. Swim or kayak at the beach in front of the house.
Walk to Sunset Beach to watch the sunset. Trying a cliff jump before the sun goes down is also a good idea.
Have dinner at the house, with a barbecue or food you bought yourself.
Walk the beach barefoot at sunrise.
Pack up in time for check-out and stop in Tagaytay on the way back.
Check-in and check-out times differ by house. One house in 2018 had check-in at 2 PM and check-out at noon, so confirm with the house you book.

items.title: From Manila by private car or rental car

children.text: The drive from Manila takes about 2–3 hours. Take SLEX and exit at Mamplasan, then follow CALAX and leave at the Tagaytay Exit. Follow the road toward Nasugbu, turn right at Palico Junction, turn right again at the roundabout onto JP Laurel Street, and continue toward Nasugbu town proper.

The other route uses CAVITEX: exit at Kawit, then pass through Tanza, Naic, Maragondon and Ternate along Antero Soriano Highway and Governor's Drive. Take the winding road before the Kaybiang Tunnel slowly, then turn toward Tali Beach Subdivision from the Ternate–Nasugbu Road.

At the fork near the entrance, go straight ahead and you will see the gate. If you enter by car you must show a vehicle pass or a copy of the authorized pass. Ask the house you booked to arrange it in advance.
Waze or Google Maps makes it easy. CALAX and the Nasugbu approach roads can jam on weekends and holidays, so leave around dawn.

items.title: From Manila by bus and local transport

children.text: Buses to Nasugbu run from Manila. According to 2019 information, people boarded at the DLTBCo terminal near LRT Buendia and the BSC terminal near EDSA Taft MRT, and the trip took 3–4 hours for about ₱160. The fare and terminals may have changed, so check.

The bus goes only as far as Nasugbu town. The community is private land, so you cannot enter it directly by public transport, and for that last stretch you have to use the vehicle of the house you booked or the tour operator.

There are day tours that run by van from Manila and back. In 2018 a package leaving from near a shopping mall cost around ₱1,199, and it included entrance fees, the tour, drinking water and a life vest.
Tour operators are often connected to property owners in the community. Check the current rate and inclusions directly with the operator.

In Nasugbu, November–April is the dry season and the remaining months are the wet season. Travel reviews also treat November–May as dry, and many recommend December–March to avoid both rain and crowds.
March–May is the Philippine summer, and visitors to the Batangas area increase. Typhoons can occasionally pass in November, so check the weather forecast before you leave.

Staying inside the community mostly means booking a beach house offered by a resident or registered member. Many people rent a whole house with several rooms, and some larger houses sleep around 20 people. Some houses have no Wi-Fi, so ask when you book. Spots are limited and walk-ins are generally not allowed, so book early for weekends and holidays.

There is no big dining strip inside the community. Cooking at the house or barbecuing with groceries you brought is common, and on day tours you either bring a packed lunch or the operator takes local orders. It is easiest to shop in Nasugbu town before going in. If you would rather stay outside the community, there are also hotels and resorts around Punta Fuego and Canyon Cove in Nasugbu, so compare them against your budget and schedule.
Confirm how to enter with your house or tour operator before you visit. If you show up without a booking, you may be stopped at the gate.
Private cars need a vehicle pass. Tell the house you booked your plate number in advance.
Check the forecast, and postpone cliff jumping and kayaking on days with rough waves.
For cliff jumping, start from the lowest level; reviews give the tip of looking at the horizon rather than down when you jump. Avoid landing near where others have just jumped.
Drones are often restricted because most houses are private property. If you do fly one, keep it low and do not fly over houses.
Bring water, sunscreen, a waterproof bag and water shoes. There are rocky sections, so water shoes are safer than sandals.
Go to Sunset Beach about 30 minutes before sunset to get a good spot. You will need a flashlight to move around after dark.
Take your trash with you and keep noise down late at night. Residents live in this community.
Tali is a private residential community, so you cannot enter without permission, and entry rules and prices change often, so check first with the place you booked.
Walk-in entry is generally not allowed. Always book a house or a tour.
Camping inside the community is generally not allowed.
Cliff jumping carries a risk of injury. Do not jump after drinking, and avoid it on days with high waves.
Do not go out into deep water without a life vest. There may be stretches where the current changes.
Keep valuables inside the house and do not leave them unattended on the beach for long.
An island off Nasugbu with Greek-style ruins, reached by boat as a day trip. Departures can be blocked by weather and rough seas, so check ahead.
A mountain climbed from a trailhead on the Ternate, Cavite side, near Nasugbu. It is said to have reopened to the public in 2023, but check the latest notice for entry rules.
A popular hiking mountain in inland Nasugbu. You can also split the beach and the mountain into two separate trips.
A highland city that makes a good rest stop on the way back to Manila. With its cafes and views, it is often recommended as the closing stop of a Tali trip.
